title: Sensors
blurb: How physical quantities become electrical signals.

topics.name: Photoresistor (LDR)
topics.question: What is a photoresistor and how do you read it
topics.assetAlt: Annotated photoresistor reference: the two LDR circuit symbols, a photo of the component, and a labelled cutaway showing the serpentine photoconductive track, electrodes, ceramic substrate and wire terminals.
topics.summary: Light-dependent resistance via a divider.

sections.heading: How it senses
paragraphs: An LDR's resistance falls as light increases — from hundreds of kΩ in darkness to a few kΩ in bright light. Wired as one leg of a voltage divider, the divider output tracks brightness.

sections.heading: Reading it
paragraphs: Feed the divider midpoint into an analog pin. A ≈10 kΩ fixed resistor gives usable swing for room lighting. The response is nonlinear, so calibrate against the conditions you care about.

topics.hint: If readings barely change between light and dark, the divider resistor is far from the LDR's working resistance — measure the LDR in your actual lighting and match it.

topics.name: Thermistor (NTC)
topics.question: What is an NTC thermistor and how do you convert it to °C
topics.assetAlt: Photo of three NTC 5D-20 thermistor discs next to a signal-conditioning schematic in which a 10 kΩ NTC thermistor and a 10 kΩ sense resistor feed the analog inputs of a precision ADC.
topics.summary: A steeply nonlinear temperature resistor.

sections.heading: Negative coefficient
paragraphs: An NTC thermistor's resistance drops as temperature rises. Like the LDR it is read through a voltage divider, but its resistance-vs-temperature curve is steep and strongly nonlinear.

sections.heading: Converting to °C
paragraphs: Do not use a linear map. Apply the Beta-parameter equation or Steinhart-Hart with the datasheet coefficients to convert resistance to temperature accurately.

topics.hint: Readings that look right at room temperature but drift badly when hot or cold mean a linear conversion — switch to the Beta equation with the part's datasheet constants.

topics.name: Tilt Ball Switch
topics.question: What is a tilt ball switch and how do you wire it
topics.assetAlt: Diagram of a tilt ball switch: a metal ball inside a tube with two wire pins; when the tube tilts, the ball slides down and bridges both contacts, shown with open- and closed-switch schematic equivalents.
topics.summary: An orientation-sensitive contact switch.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: A conductive ball rolls to bridge two contacts when tilted past a threshold, closing the circuit. It is effectively an orientation-sensitive switch — good for detecting flips, knocks or vibration.

sections.heading: Wiring
paragraphs: Treat it like any momentary switch: it needs a pull resistor for a defined open state, and benefits from software debouncing because the rolling ball chatters.

topics.hint: Multiple triggers per single tilt mean contact bounce — add INPUT_PULLUP and debounce in software (ignore changes within ≈20–50 ms).

topics.name: Strain Gauge / Load Cell
topics.question: What is a strain gauge and how does it measure force
topics.assetAlt: Labelled load-cell diagram: a metal beam bolted to a base at its fixed end, strain gauges bonded above and below the machined cutouts, and a force arrow pressing down on the free (live) end.
topics.summary: Force as a tiny resistance change.

sections.heading: How it senses
paragraphs: A bonded foil grid changes resistance slightly when stretched or compressed (its gauge factor relates ΔR/R to strain). Mounted on a flexure and wired into a Wheatstone bridge, four gauges form a load cell.

sections.heading: Conditioning the signal
paragraphs: Bridge output is on the order of millivolts per volt of excitation, so it must be amplified — a dedicated 24-bit bridge ADC (HX711) or an op-amp instrumentation stage.

topics.hint: A reading that drifts with no load change is usually thermal drift or a loose mount — use the opposite bridge arm for temperature compensation, tighten the fixture, and warm up before zeroing.

topics.name: Ultrasonic (HC-SR04)
topics.question: What is the HC-SR04 and how does time-of-flight give distance
topics.assetAlt: HC-SR04 ultrasonic module with its Vcc, Trig, Echo and GND pins labelled, beside a diagram of the transmitted sound burst reflecting off an object and returning to the receiver across the measured distance.
topics.summary: Distance from an echo round-trip.

sections.heading: Time of flight
paragraphs: A 10 µs trigger pulse fires a burst of ultrasound; the echo pin then stays HIGH for the round-trip time. Distance is `time × 343 / 2` (speed of sound, there and back).

sections.heading: Practical range
paragraphs: Reliable from roughly 2 cm to 4 m, within a cone. Soft or angled surfaces scatter the echo. It is a 5 V part with separate trigger and echo pins.

topics.hint: Distance that reads zero, max, or wildly unstable means a missed or scattered echo — aim at a flat hard surface within ≈4 m, keep the trigger at ≈10 µs, and add a timeout on pulseIn().

topics.name: Soil Moisture
topics.question: What is a capacitive soil moisture sensor and how is it calibrated
topics.assetAlt: Capacitive soil-moisture probe v2.0 with its tongue-shaped copper sensing traces (which act as a capacitor), on-board 555 timer IC, and GND, VCC and AOUT connector pins labelled.
topics.summary: Water content via dielectric constant.

sections.heading: Capacitive sensing
paragraphs: It measures the dielectric constant of the surrounding soil, which rises with water content, and outputs an analog voltage. Capacitive probes avoid the electrode corrosion that plagues resistive sensors.

sections.heading: Calibration
paragraphs: Raw readings are arbitrary, so record the value fully dry (in air) and fully wet (to the line in water) and map between them. Never submerge the electronics at the top of the board.

topics.hint: A moisture percentage that makes no sense is uncalibrated — capture the dry-in-air and wet-in-water raw values, map() between them, and keep the circuitry out of the soil.
